title: Explain the Factory design pattern (product interface, concrete products, factory), with benefits and use cases.
shortTitle: Explain the Factory design pattern with benefits and use cases
keyPoints: Factory centralises object creation behind one place so callers ask by type, never writing new.
Three parts: product interface, concrete product classes, and a factory that decides which to instantiate.
Decouples client code from concrete classes: adding a product is adding a class, not editing callers.
Supports OCP: new products are new classes with one factory registration, leaving existing code untouched.
In modern Java, a Map of Supplier replaces the switch; in Spring, injecting a Map of bean name to interface is a factory for free.
Use cases: choosing implementation by config, abstracting creation in frameworks, hiding complex construction.

s1_definition.oneliner: The Factory hides the new keyword behind one place, so callers ask for a product by type and get back an interface, and adding a new type is just adding a class.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Factory pattern** – a creational pattern that centralises object creation behind a dedicated factory so callers request a product by key instead of using `new`.
- **Three parts** – a product interface (common contract), concrete product classes (implementations), and a factory (decides which concrete product to create).
- **Decoupling** – client code depends only on the interface and the factory, not on concrete classes.
- **OCP** – adding a new product means adding a class and one factory entry; existing code is untouched.
- **Modern form** – a `Map<String, Supplier<Product>>` or Spring's `Map<String, Interface>` bean injection.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India there is one account-opening counter. Rajesh walks up and says "I want a savings account" or "I want a current account," and the clerk hands him the correct, fully prepared kit. Rajesh never goes into the back room to assemble the kit himself. The counter is the factory, the kit types are the concrete products, and the general idea of an account kit is the product interface.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Factory Pattern Structure
  ─────────────────────────

  Client                         Factory
  ──────                         ───────
  AlertService ──▶ ChannelFactory.create("SMS")
       │                           │
       │                           ▼
       │                    ┌──────────────────┐
       │                    │ NotificationChannel│ ◄── interface
       │                    └────────┬─────────┘
       │                             │
       │                  ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       │                  ▼          ▼          ▼
       │             SmsChannel EmailChannel PushChannel
       │
       ▼
  channel.send(to, msg)   ◄── works with any channel
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Factory pattern centralises object creation behind one place, so calling code asks for a product by type instead of using `new` directly. It has three parts: a product interface that defines the common contract, concrete product classes that implement it, and a factory that decides which one to create.

The benefits are decoupling, a single point of change, OCP compliance, and clean polymorphism. At National Bank of India, Rajesh had alert-sending code scattered with `new SmsChannel()` in many places. When push notifications were added, some code paths were missed and customers never got alerts. He fixed it with a `ChannelFactory`, so every alert goes through one factory. Adding WhatsApp was a new class plus one registry entry, with every existing alert untouched.

In modern Java, the factory switch is replaced by a `Map<String, Supplier<NotificationChannel>>`, and in Spring, injecting a `Map<String, NotificationChannel>` gives a factory for free. Adding a new channel is literally adding a new `@Component` bean.

The senior judgment is to use Factory when there is real variation in which concrete type to create, and to keep a plain `new` when there is no variation. Over-applying Factory adds indirection for no benefit.

Remember one sentence: Factory hides the new keyword behind one place, so callers depend only on the interface and adding a product is adding a class, not editing callers.
